#4789. We Found the Best Adjustable Dumbbells for Every Home Gym

Looking to make more gains while taking up less space? These picks from SMRTFT, PowerBlock, and REP Fitness pack a big punch in a small package.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

IF THERE'S ONE piece of home gym equipment anyone can make room for at home, it's a pair of adjustable dumbbells. These clever pieces of fitness gear require minimal space, shifting from light to heavy with a quick turn of a knob or tweak of a setting. They simplify things by tackling two challenges of working out at home: space and equipment. Think about it: A single pair of adjustable dumbbells can replace around 15 standard dumbbells.

"There's a reason dumbbells are in every single big-box gym," says MH fitness director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S., who created an arm-focused muscle-building program, All Out Arms, based heavily around dumbbells. "If you want targeted muscle—and that’s what all guys want—then you want dumbbells." Adjustable dumbbells (just like adjustable kettlebells) offer a range of weights from one compact footprint, eliminating the need for multiple sets of weights.

If you prefer working out at home (or do so out of necessity on days when you can't make it to the gym), a pair of adjustable dumbbells is a solution that helps you stay consistent with your training without leaving your home. These are effective pieces, especially when combined with cardio equipment and a great weight bench. Check out our top picks for the best adjustable dumbbells for your home gym right now.

"The Nüobell is the best blend of reliability and authentic dumbbell feel I’ve used," says Samuel, who has been using these for over three years. "The shape and design of these 'bells make them ideal for accessory motions, like skullcrushers and biceps curls, and they’re easy to hold for goblet squats too." Aside from a few scratches, they've held up great to three years of heavy use.

With a maximum weight of 80 pounds of weight per dumbbell and a feel that's nearly indistinguishable from traditional dumbbells, users can utilize the same set of weights for a complete full-body workout. Users can quickly drop down to lower weights for exercises like bent-over flies or pile on the plates for more intense squats. "It features a 'turn-and-click' design rather than just a built-in selector," notes Williams. Users simply turn the handle until they reach their desired weight.

During testing, Howell noted that the Nüobell arrived assembled and was easy to plug-and-play once unboxed. Of all the adjustable dumbbells he tried, these felt the most like actual dumbbells. "These feel like the next evolution of the traditional dumbbells we have become used to in gyms," Howell said.

The major defining features include: metal plates and handles, top-tier construction, easy click-and-go weight adjustment, and the selected weight displayed on the dumbbell itself.

However, Howell expressed some concerns about the rack it came with, feeling it might have been an afterthought. He questioned whether the tempered plastic rack would withstand the constant re-racking of the metal plates over time. Nevertheless, he emphasized that the actual dumbbells are well-crafted and feel solid as hell.

In Howell's opinion, these dumbbells are best for someone who has invested in a home gym and is serious about fitness. They are tailored for the hardcore client who likely has a squat rack and barbell in their garage as well, but wants to add an elite set of adjustable dumbbells to their training arsenal. If you’re building the mother of all home gyms and money is no object, this comprehensive premium set of dumbbells from SMRTFT might just be your best pick.

These BowFlex adjustable dumbbells adjust from 5 to 52.5 pounds in 2.5-pound increments, which replaces up to 15 pairs of dumbbells (that’s a lot of potential time and money saved). We love that the weight distribution is close to that of traditional dumbbells, and the 2.5-pound increments offer more customization in weight ranges. No matter how these BowFlex dumbbells are ordered, they arrive at your door in two separate, well-packed boxes.

The weight is adjusted through selection dials located on either side of each dumbbell. The dial system is easy to use, though not exactly as streamlined as SMRTFT's single-twist mechanism. Keep in mind that changing the weight requires docking and adjusting both sides of each dumbbell–that’s two dial adjustments for each change in weight. But I prefer them to PowerBlock dumbbells.

The previous version of the SelectTechs had a plastic casing, but these updated models now feature premium metal components that are better protected from damage. We find the design a bit wide and cumbersome for certain exercises, such as triceps extensions. "In my experience, these work best for chest-supported rows and overhead presses," says Samuel.

These dumbbells have been in regular use in my garage for half a year, I haven't had any issues with wear or tear. That said, it's essential to handle them with care and consider your exercise preferences when incorporating them into your home gym setup. Like most of the dumbbells on this list, it's probably not a great idea to drop these on the floor after finishing a set.

The last note is that advanced lifters may feel a little constrained by the 52.5-pound max weight and may want to consider the 90-pound-max-weight BowFlex Results Series SelectTech 1090s instead.

Read More: Our Review of the BowFlex Results Series SelectTech 552 Dumbbells

The NordicTrack Select-A-Weight Dumbbells are sturdy and easy to use, featuring metal plates and a robust plastic casing designed to withstand the occasional drop (though we don't recommend it). With a weight range of 10 to 55 pounds per dumbbell, adjustable in 2.5-pound increments, they cater especially well to home workouts. However, they're not our top pick for accessory movements due to their relatively broad plates.

This set arrived assembled and was ready to go once unboxed. "I appreciated that it came with a tray that gave it a home and an easy-to-store footprint," noted Howell. "Making changes in weight by 2.5-pound increments was fairly easy, and they felt really sturdy and safe even when adjusted to heavier loads—the knurled metal handle helped with this."What Howell didn't love about these was that there was no way to confirm what weight you were using once the 'bells' were removed from the rack. Only the rack is labeled with weight numbers, not the actual dumbbell."I think this is an ideal product for someone who knows their way around a gym and is looking for a solid addition to their home to supplement," says Howell. "They're perfect for an intermediate client."

In terms of sound, while "these are quieter than other adjustable dumbbells on the market, they make more noise than the PowerBlocks," explains Samuel. Additionally, if you wish to incorporate barbell movements into your home workout routine, we've found that these dumbbells work seamlessly with the Hyperbell.

One of my favorite equipment makers, I was surprised how long it took REP Fitness to come out with a viable adjustable dumbbell option. But it seems like they were waiting to create something special, and that's what they've done with the QuickDraws.

The plates can be adjusted in 2.5-pound increments, spanning from 5 to 30 pounds. For those heavy lifters, 30 pounds might not be enough, but for the average user looking for a quick pump in the arms or lighter weights for perfect accessory movements, this is a great pick. For anyone who wants to increase the weight, REP Fitness offers heavier options with the same streamlined design, for up to 60 pounds.

They've patented their Lock-N-Load adjustment system, which is straightforward and lets you change the weights by flipping a switch on each dumbbell. This system allows you to swap weights quickly, so you can change the load between dumbbell exercises and avoid stalling.

For our testing, the dumbbells arrived in two boxes and require minimal assembly, making them an ultra-accessible choice for delivery and home use.

PowerBlock adjustable dumbbells are an ultra-sturdy set designed for lasting performance, perfect for executing heavy-duty moves like dead stop rows, Romanian deadlifts, and heavy presses. At just 12 inches long with the storage stand, these dumbbells offer decent compactness and versatility.

The Pro 50 Adjustable Dumbbells cover a weight range of 5 to 50 pounds per dumbbell, with adjustments in increments of 2.5 pounds. This weight range suits beginners well, and more experienced lifters can expand the weight by opting for additional expansion kits. For those who find 50 pounds per dumbbell insufficient, PowerBlock offers heavier models such as the Elite USA (up to 90 pounds per dumbbell) or the Pro 100 EXP (up to 100 pounds per dumbbell). Most models of adjustable dumbbells by PowerBlock feature the same pin-and-lock adjustment mechanism, which is easy to use and avoids jamming issues found in some other systems.

In his testing, Howell pointed out the compact structure of the actual dumbbell, noting the plate-like weights, which are more like weighted frames than traditional circular ones. Howell found this design "genius", as the square nature of the dumbbell makes it easy to lay down once done using it without it rolling away or requiring a rack to rest it in. He also appreciated that they arrived assembled and were fairly easy to unpack and begin using.

However, Howell expressed concerns about the durability of certain components, such as the handles and the "clip" that allows you to lock your chosen weight in, which are made of plastic. He believes these dumbbells might not be robust enough for consistent use, particularly for hardcore gymgoers.

Despite these concerns, Samuel praises their adjustability and durability, stating, "I've never encountered a more durable adjustable dumbbell. I love them for farmer’s walks, heavy DB lunges, and thrusters, and rely on them anytime I do a metcon-style workout at home." Samuel also shared he’s dropped these from three or four feet up after tough sets of incline presses, "and they hold up just fine." (Although it's not advisable to make a habit of dropping any adjustable dumbbells regularly.)These dumbbells feature comfortable contoured handles that enhance grip during workouts. However, they do not provide the same weight distribution as traditional dumbbells, as Samuel points out: "If you’re looking to use a set of adjustable movements for plenty of accessory movements, go with something more dumbbell-shaped."

Look for a weight range that meets your fitness goals. Most adjustable dumbbells can be adjusted in 2.5- or 5-pound increments, so it's important to consider a weight range that fits your needs.

Adjustable dumbbells come in different shapes and sizes. Consider the size and shape of the dumbbells and make sure they feel comfortable in your hands. Basically, does the dumbbell feel "good" or natural to you? Again, this comes down to personal preference and might involve some trial and error.

Some adjustable dumbbells distribute the load differently than traditional dumbbells (atypical), changing how it responds to certain movements (particularly accessory movements). A good rule of thumb is if you're looking to perform heavier exercises (farmer's carries, RDLs, rows) you can consider an adjustable dumbbell that doesn't distribute its weight like a traditional dumbbell, such as the PowerBlock option featured above. If you're planning to do more accessory movements (like biceps curls or skull crushers), opt for a traditional dumbbell-shaped option.

There are a few different mechanisms adjustable dumbbells use to switch weights, with some being easier or more user-friendly.

This mechanism uses a dial on the end of the dumbbell handle to adjust the weight. To change the weight, you turn the dial to the desired weight, and the mechanism will lock in the appropriate weight plates. Some adjustable dumbbells must be docked in their storage base to change weight using a dial, while others can be adjusted outside their docking station.

This mechanism uses a pin to select the desired weight and can take some practice to get used to if you're new to it. To change the weight, pull out the pin, select the desired weight, then reinsert the pin into the corresponding slot to lock it in.

This mechanism uses a twist-locking mechanism to secure the weight plates. To change the weight, you twist the handle to unlock the weight plates, remove or add weight plates, and then twist the handle back to lock in the new weight.

Warranties reflect a manufacturer's confidence in its product. And with some of the best adjustable dumbbells priced at or above $500, you want to be sure your investment is protected. So, it’s important to purchase from a manufacturer that offers a clear, comprehensive warranty. They vary widely across the industry, with the most budget-forward brands offering just 90 days on some parts, and others boasting generous five-year warranties on everything. Again, the more you spend upfront, the better the warranty is likely to be. And, if there’s anything that isn’t clear to you about the stated warranty, be sure to ask. It’s your money, after all.

As the Fitness and Reviews Editor at Men's Health, it's my job to test the latest and greatest training equipment, including adjustable dumbbells. To build this guide, I tested more than 30 adjustable dumbbells over the past five years, drawing on my experience and that of my fellow MH fitness editors, including Fitness Director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S., and Senior Fitness Editor Brett Williams, NASM. Samuel utilized the top-performing adjustable dumbbells featured in this guide in fitness programs with several of his advanced clients.

We also enlisted the help of Maillard Howell of Dean CrossFit in Brooklyn, to test and assess how well these dumbbells performed in the real world (read: a high-traffic training facility). In addition, we sought insights from trainers from both our MH Advisory Board and our Strength in Diversity class for further anecdotal and experiential perspectives on the top adjustable dumbbells.

Each dumbbell was rigorously tested in a variety of categories, including durability, weight distribution, ease of shifting between weights, and aesthetics. All dumbbells were tested with three types of exercises: explosive exercises (such as cleans), multi-joint strength exercises (such as bench presses and Romanian deadlifts), and accessory movements (such as biceps curls and lateral raises). All dumbbells were also dropped from a standard bench to test baseline durability (no adjustable dumbbell should ever be dropped from shoulder height), and they were monitored for signs of rust over a three-month period.

Adjustable dumbbells pack a ton of perks compared to regular dumbbells, with the most obvious being their space-saving design: No matter which adjustable dumbbells you choose, you can guarantee they'll take up less space than the sets of traditional dumbbells they replace.

Another attractive benefit of adjustable dumbbells is that they're more cost-effective than multiple sets of traditional dumbbells. A lot of the options on this list aren't exactly budget buys, we know. But building out a weight rack with 5-15 sets of high-quality traditional dumbbells can add up in cost even quicker.

This comes down to three things: space, personal preference, and how you plan to use your dumbbells. If you have unlimited space, you can definitely consider standard dumbbells.

"If you're building out a home gym and especially if you like to train accessory motions and work through a full range of motion, you still can't beat standard dumbbells," explains Samuel.

"They're going to be more durable, have better weight distribution for most moves, and, as cool as some adjustment dial might be, there's nothing more efficient than literally putting a 35-pound dumbbell down and picking a 40-pounder up."

But if you're in tight confines or like to work out on the go, opt for a good adjustable option. "You can load a pair of Powerblocks in your trunk much more easily than you can load 10 pairs of dumbbells for a road trip."

You'll also want to consider how often you'll drop your dumbbells. Even the best, most durable adjustable dumbbells on this list still have weight-switching mechanisms and won't hold up to being routinely dropped from a few feet in the air after a set of shoulder presses as well as standard dumbbells.

The weight of adjustable dumbbells depends on your fitness level and goals. Typically, they come in two main categories: those that max out at around 50 pounds per dumbbell and those that start at 50 pounds and get way heavier.

For beginners and folks looking to engage in moderate strength training at home, a set that maxes out at 50 pounds per dumbbell should suffice. They offer a range of weights for a wide variety of exercises and are a great starting point. Beginners can work on everything from biceps curls to overhead presses to squats with these.

Now, if you're a seasoned lifter, powerlifter, or someone aiming to build strength, opt for a pair of adjustable dumbbells that can go well above 50 pounds per bell. Adjustable sets from SMRTFT can offer a max of 80 pounds and 100 pounds per bell, respectively. For experienced lifters, added weight means greater versatility in tackling heavy exercises and challenging yourself.

Just like standard dumbbells, adjustable dumbbells are safe when used correctly and with proper form. But, as with any type of fitness equipment, there are some safety considerations to keep in mind.

It's important to choose adjustable dumbbells that are well-made and constructed from durable materials. If you're using an old-school model with removable plates, make sure they're securely attached to the handle before you start your lift.

The shape, feel, and weight distribution of adjustable dumbbells can take some getting used to, depending on the model you're working with. Because they may feel different compared to standard dumbbells in movements you do regularly, it's important to focus on slow, controlled movements and proper form throughout your workout (especially as you acclimate to them).

#4788. Yamaha unveils new NMAX E, bringing electric power to its popular motorbike lineup

Yamaha is expanding its electric two-wheeler lineup with a much more capable machine, unveiling the new NMAX E as an electric version of its popular NMAX sport scooter.

The 2027 Yamaha NMAX E is being positioned as a 125cc-equivalent electric scooter, putting it firmly above the low-speed urban electric scooters that have made up much of Yamaha’s electric lineup thus far.

At its heart is Yamaha’s new compact eAxle drive unit, which sends power to the rear wheel through a belt drive. The electric motor produces 6.7 kW (9 hp) of nominal power and peaks at 7.5 kW (10 hp), along with 33.3 Nm (24.6 lb-ft) of torque.

Yamaha hasn’t published a top speed in the specifications, but the NMAX E’s A1 classification puts it in the same general category as 125cc combustion scooters rather than urban mopeds.

Power comes from a centrally mounted 3.5 kWh lithium-ion battery, which Yamaha says provides up to 104 km (65 miles) of range on the WMTC Class 1 testing cycle. The L-shaped battery is mounted low and centrally in the chassis to help maintain a low center of gravity.

Unlike many electric scooters that rely on removable batteries, the NMAX E uses a fixed pack. Yamaha has compensated for that with an onboard 800W charger, allowing riders to plug the scooter directly into a household outlet or an AC Type 2 public charging station. A full 0-100% charge takes around 5.5 hours.

Riders can choose between three riding modes. Sport (S) mode offers the quickest acceleration, Touring (T) provides smoother power delivery for everyday riding and carrying a passenger, and Eco (E) reduces acceleration and top speed while maximizing range. Regenerative braking is also included.

The rest of the scooter is fairly well equipped, including traction control, ABS, 245mm front and rear disc brakes, 13-inch wheels, a 33mm fork, dual rear shocks, and even a reverse mode to make low-speed maneuvering easier.

Nice, the Nmax has always been the premium scoot we try to get when traveling in southeast asia. Always felt like it would've been even better electrified. No removable battery seems a bit of a miss. That might constrain a big chunk of demand.

A five-inch TFT display includes smartphone connectivity through Yamaha’s Motor On app, providing turn-by-turn navigation as well as battery status, ride information, maintenance reminders, and other connected features. There’s also keyless ignition, USB-C charging, LED lighting, and illuminated underseat storage large enough for a full-face helmet, depending on its size.

Perhaps most importantly, the NMAX E looks like a proper Yamaha scooter rather than an electric experiment. Its dual headlights and distinctive side panels closely follow the styling language of Yamaha’s existing MAX family.

That could prove important as established motorcycle manufacturers increasingly attempt to bring electric models into their existing lineups rather than treating them as separate curiosities.

Pricing and exact market availability haven’t yet been announced, but Yamaha is positioning the NMAX E as a 2027 model for the European market.

#4787. Maximo milestone: friendly robot has completed 300,000 tasks

After completing the first half of Amazon’s Bellefield complex last summer, Maximo engineers have put their helpful robot friend into high gear, with the latest version 3.0 robot-equipped construction crews installing as many as 24 solar panel modules per hour, per person. And now, the company is reporting that Maximo has completed its 300,000th construction task. (!)

If that 24 modules per hour, per person rate sounds fast, that’s because it is. At full tilt, the latest Maximo robot-equipped crews have nearly doubled the output of traditional installation methods at similar solar locations throughout Southern California. Now, with 300,000 tasks under its belt, the robot is proving to be both fast and durable.

“The future of solar construction depends on bringing together the experience of our people and new technology,” explains Matt Tetrault, President of Primoris’ Renewables business.

Like just about everyone these days, Maximo is playing up its machines’ NVDIVIA hardware, re-branding its robots’ repetitive automation as “physical AI.” That’s not to say the robots don’t work, however – as their deployment at Amazon’s Bellefield solar field is proving.

(By) leveraging NVIDIA AI infrastructure together with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries and NVIDIA Isaac Sim open robotics simulation framework, the Maximo team was able to develop, test and refine robotic capabilities through physics-based simulation and AI driven modeling before deploying updates in the field. The combination of AI, vision, robotics and simulation driven engineering reduced development and validation timelines and increased confidence in field performance as the robotic fleet scaled.

Amazon Web Services (AWS) powered the development, deployment, and operation of Maximo’s AI-driven field systems. AWS provides scalable computing, automated software delivery, and advanced data analytics, including real-time construction intelligence, enabling Maximo to collect operational robotics data and continuously improve performance.

The rapid deployment of solar panels at utility scale projects like this one, which is set to eventually reach over a GW of solar generating capacity, will help companies like Amazon reduce their carbon footprint, of course – but also save them big money as the price of fossil fuels continues to climb.

So Primoris’ Renewables is the name of a business, Maximo is the name of a solar robotics company incubated by The AES Corporation. Maximo makes a robot (also called Maximo I think) using NVDIVIA hardware and software, and also AWS cloud software, and Bellefield is a solar field owned by Amazon. Or so I gather so far.

The Maximo team says it has plans to extend its robots potential use cases beyond solar and into construction tasks that require similar pick and place and feeding and attaching movements, site logistics, and site cleanup. And like just about every other business that demands a high degree of physical labor, the construction industry is facing huge labor shortages, making machines like Maximo that provide real efficiency gains welcome additions to the job site.

#4785. Hormone Therapy May Boost Weight Loss on Wegovy, But Not as Much on Zepbound

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Females using menopause hormone therapy (MHT) alongside GLP-1 medications such as Ozempic or Wegovy may experience greater weight loss, according to a study presented at the 2026 Annual Meeting of the Menopause Society.

Weight gain is a common concern among middle-aged women. While much of this is associated with aging, hormonal changes during menopause can also contribute to changes in body fat and its distribution.

GLP-1 medications have been shown to be effective for weight loss. However, the results may vary by sex and reproductive stage.

For example, studies have found that women and adults under age 55 may experience greater weight loss with these medications.

A previous small observational study in postmenopausal women found that using MHT alongside semaglutide, the active ingredient in Ozempic and Wegovy, was associated with greater weight loss.

However, whether hormone therapy influences weight loss outcomes with different GLP-1 medications remains unclear.

To investigate this question, researchers compared weight loss in middle-aged women receiving either semaglutide or tirzepatide, with or without MHT. The findings have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal.

The study included 3,855 women with an average age of 57 and an average body mass index (BMI) of 36 kg/m2.

The semaglutide cohort included 2,379 individuals, while the tirzepatide cohort included 1,476 individuals.

The average follow-up in the semaglutide cohort, both with and without MHT, was 26 months. The average follow-up in the tirzepatide group was 17 months for those using MHT and 16 months for those not using it.

The researchers found that in the semaglutide cohort, those using MHT alongside the GLP-1 medication had significantly greater weight loss at 9 months than those not using MHT.

These differences were sustained at 12 and 15 months and at the final follow-up. Those using MHT were also more likely to reach up to a 30% total body weight loss than those not using it.

In the tirzepatide cohort, those using MHT had a modestly greater weight loss at 3 months and were more likely to achieve more than 5% total body weight loss by the final follow-up. However, no significant difference in weight loss was observed at later time points.

These findings suggest that MHT use may be associated with greater weight loss among middle-aged women taking semaglutide. However, the researchers did not observe a sustained, statistically significant difference in weight loss among those taking tirzepatide.

Betul Hatipoglu, MD, Director of the Diabetes and Obesity Center at the University Hospitals Cleveland Medical Center, who was not involved in the study, told Healthline that the findings are encouraging.

However, she also cautioned that people should be careful not to interpret them as evidence that hormone therapy should be added to GLP-1 treatment specifically to enhance weight loss.

“This is an association, and the study provides an opportunity to discuss how menopause, aging, changes in body composition, and metabolic health can be present,” she said.

It is important to keep in mind that the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved certain hormone therapy medications to treat menopause symptoms such as hot flashes, night sweats, and vaginal dryness. However, these medications are not FDA-approved for weight loss or obesity management.

The study authors noted that larger studies are needed to confirm their observations and to inform individualized strategies for middle-aged females.

Sherry Ross, MD, board certified OB-GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who was not involved in the study, noted that weight gain is one of the most common concerns she hears from women during menopause. Beyond affecting self-esteem and quality of life, excess abdominal fat can increase the risk of type 2 diabetes and heart disease.

“Finding effective, sustainable ways to manage weight is important for women’s long-term health and healthy aging,” she said.

“I would like to see prospective, randomized studies examining GLP-1 medications with and without hormone therapy to determine whether hormone therapy directly improves weight loss and helps women maintain it over time. In the meantime, treatment decisions should be individualized and guided by a healthcare professional.”

Ross advised that the decision should be based on your individual symptoms, health history, and treatment goals.

“Hormone therapy can significantly improve disruptive menopausal symptoms, including hot flashes, sleep disturbances, and mood changes. By helping women feel better and more energetic, it may also make it easier to exercise and manage their weight,” she said.

Hatipoglu noted that GLP-1-based medications, on the other hand, are effective treatments for obesity and can improve important aspects of metabolic health. Their use should be based on an individual’s weight-related health risks, medical history, and treatment goals.

“For a woman who has both bothersome menopausal symptoms and obesity, it may be entirely appropriate to consider both treatments. But I would not recommend starting hormone therapy solely to improve the weight-loss response to a GLP-1 medication based on the evidence currently available,” she said.

“It is also important to remember that successful weight management during and after menopause is about more than the number on the scale. Preserving muscle mass, maintaining bone health, improving metabolic health, and supporting long-term physical function are equally important.”

You should speak with your healthcare professional about the risks and benefits of all treatment options.

#4783. Former CAKE team is back in the kitchen with a new electric motorcycle

If the new ReBake Abler electric motorcycle looks like it might share a bit of DNA with Sweden’s dearly departed CAKE, there’s a good reason for that.

ReBake Motors has officially unveiled its first electric two-wheeler at EICMA 2026 in Milan, introducing the Abler as a highly modular, utility-focused electric moped and light motorcycle.

Behind the new Swedish company is founder and CEO Karl Ytterborn, who spent eight years at CAKE from its founding in 2016 through 2024. CAKE famously built some of the most interesting minimalist electric motorcycles and utility bikes on the market before ultimately collapsing after failing to secure additional funding. Ytterborn says ReBake is intended to apply many of the lessons learned during that experience, while eliminating unnecessary cost and complexity.

Its chunky 42mm aluminum tube frame isn’t just a styling exercise. ReBake designed it as a mounting system, allowing cargo accessories to attach directly to the frame at multiple locations. That means riders can configure the bike for everything from carrying groceries and passengers to more serious utility duties.

There are two versions. The Abler45 is an EU L1e-B moped with a 45 km/h (28 mph) top speed, 4 kW nominal motor and 5.12 kW peak output. It starts at €3,990 including VAT.

The €4,990 Abler80 steps up to the A1 light motorcycle category, increasing nominal power to 6.14 kW and peak power to 7.68 kW while pushing the top speed beyond 80 km/h (50 mph). Both versions use a direct-drive rear hub motor.

Energy comes from removable 2 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries weighing 17 kg (37.5 lb) apiece. The Abler45 comes standard with one battery but can carry two, while the Abler80 includes two for 4 kWh of total capacity. With both batteries, ReBake claims up to 160 km (99 miles) of low-speed urban range on the Abler45 or 114 km (71 miles) on the Abler80. Each battery can be charged either on or off the bike from a normal 230V outlet, reaching a full charge in four hours.

The rest of the hardware includes 14-inch cast wheels, 140mm of front suspension travel, dual rear shocks, front and rear disc brakes with combined braking, regenerative braking, and full LED lighting.

Perhaps more interesting than any individual specification, though, is simply seeing another Swedish electric motorcycle startup emerge from CAKE’s ashes.

CAKE demonstrated that there was plenty of appetite for unconventional, lightweight electric motorcycles. Unfortunately, it also demonstrated just how difficult it is to turn that enthusiasm into a sustainable business.

ReBake appears to be getting another crack at that equation – this time with eight years’ worth of lessons already baked in.

#4781. Tesla wins trade zone status for Texas Megapacks, but China tariffs stay

Tesla’s Megapack factory in Brookshire, Texas, is now officially a foreign-trade zone, a US customs program that lets manufacturers defer duties on imported parts. The FTZ Board’s approval, published in the Federal Register on Monday, runs for 14 months.

It’s easy to read this as Tesla getting a pass on tariffs for the Chinese LFP cells inside its Megapacks. Tesla’s own application says otherwise: parts hit by Section 301, 232, or 122 tariffs still pay them.

Tesla filed the request on May 20 for Subzone 84AM, part of FTZ 84 in the Houston area. That’s the factory where Tesla started Megapack 3 production in August, with a planned capacity of 50 GWh per year.

The application lists roughly 80 imported components Tesla wants to bring in under zone procedures, from coolant pumps and transformers to busbars, wiring harnesses, circuit boards and battery cells. Duty rates on those parts go up to 6.5%, while finished Megapacks and Bento inverters range from duty-free to 3.4%.

That gap is the usual reason companies set up an FTZ. A manufacturer in a zone can normally elect to pay the finished product’s lower rate instead of the rate on each imported part.

But the application spells out the limit. Components subject to duties under Section 122 of the Trade Act, Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act, or Section 301 “require subject merchandise to be admitted to FTZs in privileged foreign status,” according to the notice.

Privileged foreign status locks in a part’s own classification and tariff treatment when it enters the zone. So a Chinese LFP cell that ends up in a Megapack sold in the US still pays the Section 301 tariff on Chinese non-EV lithium-ion batteries, which jumped from 7.5% to 25% on January 1, 2026. Tesla just pays it later, when the finished Megapack leaves the zone.

Here’s what Tesla actually gets out of it:

The approval came with the same wording the FTZ Board has used all year. Production was “authorized on a limited basis,” and “further subject to a fourteen-month time period.”

Tesla got an identical decision for Megapack and inverter production at Fremont, Livermore and Lathrop in California this summer, with a one-year limit instead. Eastman Chemical, battery pack maker Rose Batteries, and chipmaker Qorvo all received similar time-limited, “limited basis” approvals in 2026.

The 14-month clock puts the expiry around the end of 2027. That’s roughly when LG Energy Solution is due to start supplying Tesla with LFP cells from Michigan under a $4.3 billion contract for Megapack 3, with mass production expected in the second half of 2027.

Tesla hasn’t hidden the issue. When tariffs escalated in April 2025, CFO Vaibhav Taneja said the impact on energy storage would be “outsized since we source lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery cells from China.” We wrote at the time that Tesla’s only growing business was kneecapped by Trump’s tariffs.

Tesla has since brought up its own LFP cell factory in Nevada, but Taneja said it would only cover a fraction of Tesla’s installed capacity. And Brookshire alone is designed for 50 GWh a year, on top of the 40 GWh Lathrop factory in California.

Tesla’s Megapacks are bringing big batteries to the grid, but you can get the same benefits at home by pairing solar with storage. #4779. I Am Turning 40, and Refusing to Apologize for It

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 12, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

Yes, I celebrate the month. (Don’t @ me!) It was actually something I started doing in college. My birthday (the actual day) falls close to Thanksgiving, so many of my friends would be leaving campus right around the time I was getting ready to celebrate. I also had a roommate whose birthday was close to Christmas, so we started celebrating early.

The trend caught on (whether it caught on or I pushed it, I will never know). This worked well until my 21st birthday, which, as we all know, cannot legally be celebrated early—at least not if you want your special bar drink in hand.

If you’re rolling your eyes and thinking I appear a bit arrogant, bear with me for a moment while I explain. While celebrating and having fun with friends was, of course, fun, these celebrations actually served a deeper purpose for me—although I didn't know it at the time. When college ended, I found myself alone again, thrown back into a world where my only source of support—my family—was unsafe and unstable. Home was scary.

Celebrating myself became a way of honoring my own journey. It was a way of recognizing the strength it took to navigate the year, and the safety I was learning to create within myself. It became a "Yay, Kaytee, you made it another year. You did it." Years later, I still have that same message, but it has become something deeper.

This was almost 20 years ago. This month I turn 40. An age where we, especially women, are told to stop celebrating. An age we are taught to dread. All month, I’ve received messages like these from others, including my own family:

“I bet you’re not excited about this birthday.”

"I was going to send you a card, but I imagine you don't want the reminder."

“I bet you won’t celebrate the whole month anymore.”

And I can’t help but wonder: Why? Why are we so negative about aging? We mourn when people die young, yet somehow shame those of us who are fortunate enough to keep living. We grieve the years someone never got to experience, while simultaneously treating the years we do get as something to fear.

I refuse to participate in this ageism. I have always celebrated my birthday, and I always will. Not just in the traditional, celebratory sense (I mean, cake is always nice), but as a way of honoring myself and all that I have become. I am always stumped at how much it bothers people that I dare embrace myself as an aging woman.

I am proud of who I am today. I love myself more today than I ever did when I was young. I no longer self-medicate or mistreat my body in the ways I had to to survive my childhood. I am happier and healthier now than I ever have been before. I have come so far and learned so much since that 20-year-old college student who celebrated her birthday with her roommates for a week straight, in one of the few places where she felt safe (but was unable to verbalize this at the time). I wish I could go back and tell her that someday it won't be so scary, and she won't have to put on a fake persona of strength to continue the denial. I would tell her not only that she would survive, but how much she would survive, and how much of a life she would eventually build for herself. I think she would be pretty damn proud, too. (And maybe a bit relieved to see a light at the end of what felt like a long, dark tunnel.)

Happy birthday month to me. And to all of us who have survived and are surviving. I hope you find a way to honor and celebrate yourself, too.

#4777. This Is How Fast You Should Walk to Help Lower Your Risk of Death

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

New research shows that how fast you walk, whether measured in a clinical test or through daily activity, can help predict your risk of dying from any cause.

The study compared two ways of measuring walking: a short walking speed test conducted in a clinic and the step rate people take in their everyday lives, measured with a wrist-worn device.

Both measures were linked to mortality risk and showed similar ability to predict it.

The findings, published on October 23 in JAMA Network Open, could help doctors and researchers choose the best method for assessing health risks in different settings.

The study was part of the Whitehall II accelerometer substudy in the United Kingdom.

It included 4,067 participants, mostly males, with an average age of about 69 years. About one-third of the subjects were female.

The researchers collected data from January 2012 to December 2013 and followed up through August 2024.

To measure clinical walking speed, participants completed a standard walking test. They walked a marked 2.44-meter course at their usual pace. The test was repeated three times, and the average speed in meters per second was used for analysis. Participants who normally used a cane were allowed to use it during the test.

For free-living walking measurements, participants wore a wrist-worn GENEActiv accelerometer for 9 consecutive days. This device recorded movement at a high frequency and used special software to detect walking episodes and count steps.

From this data, two key measures of walking cadence were calculated: the median walking cadence (the middle value of steps per minute during walking periods) and the 95th-percentile walking cadence (a higher step rate indicating brisk walking). The study also calculated the average number of daily steps.

The researchers additionally gathered information on factors known to affect mortality, such as:

National death records were used to identify deaths during the follow-up period.

Statistical methods were then used to estimate the risk of death associated with walking speed and cadence while accounting for other risk factors.

The models were adjusted step-by-step: starting with no adjustments, then adding sociodemographic factors, behavioral factors, and finally health-related factors.

The ability of walking measures to predict mortality was assessed using a statistical measure.

The study also examined differences between males and females.

The researchers additionally conducted analyses to test how well the results held up when they excluded early deaths, looked at subgroups by age and health status, and used different definitions of walking cadence.

During a median follow-up of nearly 12 years, 739 participants died.

The average clinical walking speed of participants was 1.2 meters per second. The median walking cadence during daily life was about 75 steps per minute, and the 95th percentile walking cadence was about 112 steps per minute.

The study found only a weak correlation between clinical walking speed and free-living walking cadence, meaning the two measures do not strongly reflect the same walking behavior. However, both measures were independently associated with a lower risk of death.

After adjusting for age, sex, lifestyle, and health factors, for every standard increase in clinical walking speed, the risk of death was 23% lower.

Similarly, higher median and 95th-percentile walking cadences were associated with 17% and 18% lower risks of death, respectively.

When examining how well these walking measures predicted mortality, each on its own showed modest predictive ability.

Adding clinical walking speed to a model with other known risk factors slightly improved mortality prediction, while adding free-living walking cadence also improved prediction, albeit to a similar degree to that of clinical walking speed.

Combining clinical walking speed with free-living walking parameters provided a small boost in predictive ability, but the effect was not significant after accounting for detailed health factors.

The study also found that walking speed and cadence had similar predictive power for both men and women, although the overall prediction models performed slightly better for women.

Several sensitivity analyses supported the main findings. Results were consistent when excluding early deaths, focusing on healthier or older participants, and using different ways to define walking cadence.

Overall, this study suggests that clinical walking speed tests and free-living walking cadence measurements from wrist-worn devices are both useful in predicting all-cause mortality risk. They provide similar information but reflect different aspects of walking behavior.

The choice between methods may depend on the purpose of the assessment, available resources, and the context in which the measurement is taken.

Neha Sabharwal, PT, DPT, a physical therapist and director of rehabilitation specializing in geriatric mobility and functional decline at Vintage Faire Nursing and Rehabilitation Center in Modesto, CA, said that walking speed helps predict longevity because it’s an indicator of someone’s overall health.

“Walking is something most of us do without thinking about it, but it requires several body systems to work together,” she told Healthline. “Your heart and lungs have to keep up, your muscles need to produce enough force, and your brain has to coordinate each step while keeping you balanced.”

Sabharwal, who wasn’t involved in the study, said that in her work, she pays attention to when someone starts walking more slowly than before.

“It is easy to dismiss that change as part of getting older, but there may be something else going on,” she said. This could include muscle weakness, pain, reduced endurance, balance problems, or underlying medical conditions.

According to Sabharwal, the current study is valuable because it suggests that useful information about people’s movement can be obtained outside a clinical setting.

However, she cautioned against misinterpreting the findings to mean that simply walking faster will make you live longer.

“People who naturally walk faster may already have better underlying health,” said Sabharwal.

“I would be less concerned about whether someone walks faster than their neighbor and more interested in whether they are walking slower than they did six months ago,” she said.

Theodore Strange, MD, chairman of medicine at Northwell Staten Island University Hospital and senior vice president of the Metro Market Region at Northwell Health, shared some insights for those who may notice their walking speed has declined. Strange wasn’t involved in the study.

“I mean, if it’s slowing down because a week or two ago, you were walking up a flight of steps with no problem, and now, you’re having some shortness of breath, I think it should be evaluated,” he told Healthline.

Strange added that if you’re experiencing aches or pains that weren’t there before, you should consult a healthcare professional, as they can make exercise more difficult.

It’s also essential to manage any chronic diseases that you have so that you can exercise as well as possible within the constraints of your condition, he said.

“And I think slow and steady wins the race here,” said Strange. He suggests monitoring your walking with a device like a pedometer and progressively increasing your steps.

“Everybody talks about 10,000 steps a day. I think the most recent studies show probably 7,000 to 8,000 is adequate,” he said. You can start where you are and work your way up gradually.

Strange further noted that physical therapy can sometimes be helpful if you have issues with gait mechanics, balance, or strength. Additionally, you might benefit from exercise that is tailored to your condition, for example, if you’ve had a stroke.

Finally, Strange advised stretching before and after exercise to keep your muscles moving.

“I go back to adequate nutrition and hydration being important,” he said. You want to make sure you are adequately supporting your body’s ability to exercise, said Strange.

#4776. The Universality of Privilege and Inheritance of Excellence

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 12, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

The word privilege has somehow evolved linguistically to be viewed negatively. It has also come to imply an unearned advantage or an unfair benefit held by one group at another's expense.

Throughout human history, privilege has meant something quite different: privilege has emerged when individuals and/or groups apply merit, achievement, competence, and excellence in ways that expand possibilities for everyone. I refer to this as the MACE Principle.

Research shows that high levels of expertize and exceptional performance emerge through sustained practice, learning, and skill refinement rather than arising spontaneously. In this sense, such accomplishments and the benefits they create for subsequent generations are among the oldest features of human civilization (Ericsson, 2008; Srivastava & Das, 2015).

Nearly three million years ago, our distant ancestors fashioned the first stone tools. The first person to shape stone into a cutting implement created something far more significant than a simple object. That innovation gave the entire group a practical advantage.

The collective also gained a privilege. The tribe could now cut hunted and gathered food and, self-evidently, share their food far more efficiently and much more quickly. Survival itself became easier.

Consequently, the privilege created by that stone-tool innovation was not confined to the inventor; it became a significant benefit and privilege enjoyed by the collective (Kivell, 2015; Stout, 2011).

The same pattern recurs throughout history. The invention of the wheel transformed transport and trade. Once developed, the wheel's benefits and the privilege it created extended far beyond its creator.

Entire communities far removed from the original invention gained the privilege of moving goods and people more efficiently. What began as an achievement of human ingenuity became a shared privilege and an immense social advantage beyond its original location (Kivell, 2015; Stout, 2011).

Perhaps no invention demonstrates this process more dramatically than the printing press. Developed in the 15th century by Johannes Gutenberg in Mainz, within the Holy Roman Empire (present-day Germany), the printing press fundamentally altered humanity's relationship with the development and advancement of knowledge.

Reading, writing, collective information, ideas, and knowledge, once largely confined to a comparatively small number of individuals, could now be reproduced, preserved, and distributed on a scale that was never before possible.

Reading and writing ceased to be “a mystery” for a select number of individuals or a “select” group. As with the stone tool and the wheel before it, the printing press created new benefits and privileges, consequently moving these benefits and privileges from the few to the many.

Although history informs us (as with all inventions and achievements), the resulting benefits and privileges were not always distributed equally.

However, even with this being the case, with the wider dissemination of knowledge (following the invention of the 15th-century printing press), the benefits of this invention extended far beyond Gutenberg and transformed what future generations could achieve (Jara-Figueroa et al., 2019; Triggle & Triggle, 2017).

Consider what followed. For approximately three million years, humanity crafted tools, built settlements, established civilizations, constructed cities, developed metallurgy, crossed oceans, fought wars, and created empires.

During this period, countless innovations delivered immense benefits and privilege. Yet the accumulation and transmission of knowledge remained comparatively limited.

Then, within about five centuries of the invention of the printing press, humanity witnessed an unprecedented acceleration in the growth and development of knowledge (Jara-Figueroa et al., 2019; Triggle & Triggle, 2017).

In the 18th century, Edward Jenner laid the foundations of modern immunization with the first successful smallpox vaccination (Riedel, 2005).

In the 20th century, the United States sent three men to the Moon: Neil Armstrong, the first human to walk on its surface; Buzz Aldrin, the second; and Michael Collins, who remained in lunar orbit as part of the mission.

These achievements produced further benefits and privilege, as earlier innovations had. They reflected humanity's expanding capacity to preserve, transmit, and build upon knowledge. The printing press transformed reading, writing, ideas, and information into a far more widely shared social benefit and privilege for the many (Triggle & Triggle, 2017).

In doing so, it expanded the benefits and privilege available to successive generations and helped create the conditions for scientific, technological, and civilizational advancement to proceed at a pace previously unknown in human history (Jara-Figueroa et al., 2019; Triggle & Triggle, 2017).

The same principle applied across medicine, engineering, agriculture, chemistry, and countless other fields.

Vaccines, clean water systems, supermarkets, automobiles, telecommunications, digital technologies, and now artificial intelligence all exist because individuals pursued excellence in their respective domains.

The benefits of those achievements are enjoyed not merely by their creators but by millions, and even potentially billions, of people (Tewksbury et al., 1980; Yu & Liu, 2021).

Throughout history, parents have generally sought to provide advantages, opportunities, benefits, and privilege to their children, just as previous generations sought to provide them to those who followed.

Civilization itself can therefore be understood as the cumulative result of countless individuals attempting to improve the circumstances inherited by the next generation (Gulyas & Powell, 2019; Stout & Hecht, 2017).

This does not self-evidently mean that every benefit or privilege is distributed equally; it never has and it never will.

It does mean, however, that inventions and achievements, no matter what they were, enriched lives, from the smallest tribes to the largest civilizations, because there were individuals who invented something that changed what previously existed, and with this, benefits and privilege arose (Dean et al., 2014; Tewksbury et al., 1980).

The story of human civilization is the story of expanding everyone's potential for privilege, but not a guarantee. Through innovation, discovery, and excellence, however, humanity has repeatedly turned extraordinary achievements into benefits that potentially eventually become available to the broader populace.

The greatest privilege is that each generation inherits the achievements of those who came before and can contribute new ones for those yet to come (Dean et al., 2014; Stout & Hecht, 2017).

#4775. This electric microcar just got a 50 mph upgrade, plus a secret Turbo mode

The adorable little Eli ZERO electric microcar is growing up. At this year’s EICMA motorcycle show in Milan, Eli Electric Vehicles is unveiling a faster, more powerful version of its pint-sized electric car, along with a sporty new limited-edition model that even includes a hidden Turbo mode.

First teased last week, the new Eli ZERO MX is the company’s first L7e-class electric vehicle, allowing it to reach speeds of up to 80 km/h (50 mph). That’s a significant jump from the 45 km/h (28 mph) top speed of the original L6e version that we originally reviewed, opening the door to a much wider range of driving scenarios.

And perhaps most importantly, the company managed to squeeze that extra performance into the same tiny package.

The Eli ZERO MX retains the original’s ultra-compact 2.25-meter (7.4-foot) length, making it considerably smaller than even the smallest conventional passenger cars.

But under that tiny exterior, the MX now packs up to 20 kW (27 hp) of peak power, compared to the 12 kW (16 hp) of the original Eli ZERO.

The upgraded model also features a 14.4 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery, providing a claimed range of up to 200 km (124 miles) per charge.

That’s a pretty respectable figure for a vehicle designed primarily for short urban and suburban trips.

The rear-wheel-drive microcar features selectable ECO and SPORT driving modes, a 30% climbing capability, and a tight 7.2-meter turning circle. Charging is handled by a 3.3 kW onboard charger, allowing owners to plug in at home or use public AC charging stations.

Despite its diminutive size, the Eli ZERO MX also includes a surprisingly long list of features normally associated with much larger cars.

Those include air conditioning and heating, a panoramic moonroof, soft-close doors, keyless entry and start, electric power steering, ABS, front and rear disc brakes, and an electronic parking brake.

There’s also an 8.8-inch digital instrument cluster, a reversing camera with rear radar, and an optional 10.1-inch infotainment display with Apple CarPlay.

The MX is available in four colors: Pearl White, Arctic Silver, Graphite, and Champagne.

The biggest difference, though, is the vehicle’s classification. While the original Eli ZERO falls under Europe’s L6e light quadricycle category, the new MX qualifies as an L7e heavy quadricycle. That means it generally requires a higher-level driving license, but also allows for considerably more performance.

For drivers who love the idea of a tiny electric runabout but need something capable of keeping up with faster suburban traffic, the MX could be a much more compelling option.

Eli isn’t stopping at a faster version of its microcar.

The company is also introducing the Eli ZERO Race Edition, a limited-production model available in both the original L6e and the new L7e configurations.

Finished in an exclusive Turbo Red paint job, the Race Edition features racing stripes across the hood, roof, and body panels, along with a rear spoiler and special wheel badging.

Inside, the sporty treatment continues with a two-tone Race Red microsuede and light gray interior, including special upholstery, dashboard accents, and embroidered seats.

But the most interesting feature isn’t immediately visible.

Eli has included a secret Turbo mode activated by pressing and holding the hazard light button. After four quick chimes, the digital instrument cluster switches to Turbo mode and the car’s acceleration response becomes sharper.

Importantly, the feature doesn’t increase the vehicle’s top speed or exceed its regulatory performance limits. Instead, it changes the way the car responds to accelerator inputs, giving it a sportier driving feel.

It’s a fun little Easter egg in a vehicle that already has plenty of personality.

Eli is also offering a new Carbon Aero Kit, consisting of a carbon fiber front splitter, side skirts, and rear wing. The kit is compatible with both the Race Edition and other Eli ZERO models.

Eli has spent years developing its vision of a smaller, lighter, and more efficient alternative to conventional cars, particularly for the short trips that make up much of our daily driving.

The company has already launched its second-generation Eli ZERO, which shares the same 96V electrical architecture and aluminum chassis as the new MX.

By expanding into the L7e category, Eli is addressing one of the biggest limitations of its original design: speed.

A 28 mph (45 km/h) microcar makes plenty of sense in dense urban centers, but its usefulness quickly drops off when drivers need to venture onto faster roads. A 50 mph (80 km/h) version, on the other hand, could make the same tiny vehicle practical for considerably more people.

In the US, this could go pretty much anywhere that didn't require highway driving. Perfect one-and-a-halfth car.

The Eli ZERO family is currently available through authorized dealers in several European markets, including Italy, Norway, and the Netherlands, with prices starting at €10,500 (approximately US $12,000) for the base model. Pricing for the new MX and Race Edition hasn’t yet been announced.

Eli also has a pilot program underway in the United States, though the new models are being introduced primarily for the European market.

Both the Eli ZERO MX and Race Edition will be on display at EICMA 2026 in Milan from November 3–8.

For a vehicle that takes up less than half the space of a conventional car, the Eli ZERO is certainly finding ways to make a bigger impression!

#4774. Do you need a preventative rabies vaccine? Probably not.

Published Nov 3, 2026 8:07 AM EST

Of all the deadly diseases that can spread from mammals to humans, rabies is the most infamous. Cujo had it. Old Yeller had it. A squirrel in “National Lampoon’s Christmas Vacation” had it. Unfortunately, this virus doesn’t only live in fiction. It kills at least 59,000 people a year and is present in over 150 countries. On that list is the U.S., which is seeing a nationwide surge in reported cases of human exposures to rabid or possibly rabid animals.

If left untreated, rabies is always fatal (both for animals and humans). On the bright side, it’s also 100 percent preventable. Typically, in the U.S., humans get vaccinated for rabies after suspected rabies exposure, but right now many of us are wondering: Can and should you get vaccinated against rabies just as a precaution? Is there any benefit in getting a preventative rabies vaccine? The simple answer is no. Getting a pre-exposure vaccine doesn’t protect you from contracting the disease, and if you have an encounter with an animal that might have rabies, you’ll still need to get follow up doses regardless.

Before diving in, let’s clear up some common misconceptions about rabies and the rabies vaccine. Rabies is a zoonotic virus that comes in two types: furious rabies and paralytic rabies. Both types of rabies attack the central nervous system and both are fatal. Any mammal can be infected with rabies, and if infected, can transmit it to other animals or humans through a bite or scratch—even if you can’t see or feel the wound. Though rabies doesn’t turn its victims into people-eating zombies, as Hollywood would have us believe, it does deliver an acutely agonizing death.

The modern vaccine for rabies is made from cell culture. A cell culture vaccine contains no live virus. It is literally impossible for you to get rabies from the vaccine, which, you may be surprised to hear, is also pretty painless.

“The rabies vaccine is no more painful than a flu shot,” Dr. Edward R. Rensimer, a board-certified doctor of infectious diseases and internal medicine and director of the International Medicine Center in Houston, tells Popular Science.

If exposed to a rabid or possibly rabid animal, you will require more than one dose of a rabies vaccine.

“The injection site and number of doses recommended are dependent on the type of exposure you’ve had to a potentially rabid animal,” says Dr. Mirava Yuson, an epidemiologist and postdoctoral researcher working at the UCLA TIDE (Translational Infectious Disease Eco-epidemiology) Lab.

“You can expect, for example, that a bite wound induced by an animal that’s suspected to be rabid, versus a light scratch from an animal that is not suspected to have rabies, will merit different doses and numbers of recommended boosters that are needed to complete a vaccine series.”

Both Yuson and Rensimer cannot overstate the safety and efficacy of the rabies vaccine and emphasize that side effects, should they occur, are minimal.

“It is analogous to the flu vaccine,” Rensimer says, adding that in his more than 45 years of administering the vaccine he’s never seen a major adverse event.

“A very small minority of people in the 24 hours after the first dose may have low-grade fever, body aches, and malaise.”

So, the rabies vaccine is a totally safe, 100 percent effective, and generally gentle vaccine? Sign us up! In all seriousness, why wouldn’t we get this vaccine, regardless of exposure risk, especially now, when rabies outbreaks and mass rabies exposure events are on the rise across the U.S.? Turns out there are a couple reasons why getting the rabies vaccine without any known risk exposure doesn’t make sense.

First, the “better safe than sorry” approach doesn’t work with rabies. Getting a rabies shot before a risk exposure event does not prevent you from becoming infected with rabies, nor does it minimize the effects of the fatal virus should you get it. You will still die if untreated by vaccinations post-exposure.

“There is a pre-exposure rabies vaccine that people get before traveling to rabies-endemic areas; however, the problem is, even if you get it, the minute you are exposed to a potentially rabid animal, you need a second dose, the post-exposure vaccine,” Yuson says.

“Veterinary professionals like me get them every year, but that does not preclude us from needing a post-exposure dose should we be potentially exposed. One vaccine is never enough and that is supremely important to know.”

Inside the school where dogs learn to sniff out bed bugs and other pests

Why do dogs’ legs shake during pets? It’s not because they like it.

Could a whale really swallow a human? We asked a biologist.

Second, getting a rabies vaccine regardless of risk exposure could confuse your case for clinicians if you do eventually face potential risk exposure.

“Getting the vaccine without known risk exposure can unfortunately cause some issues with the next dose should you be exposed or possibly exposed to a rabid animal,” Yuson says. “It becomes a question [for doctors]: ‘Do we start the regimen all over?’”

The best way to stay safe is also a bit of a bummer: It’s to limit contact with wildlife. All mammals are capable of getting infected with and transmitting rabies. In the U.S., there are infected raccoons, foxes, skunks and, most of all, bats, which are responsible for 70 percent of rabies deaths in people.

“The thing with bats, without getting too technical, is that they’re the only flying mammals,” Yuson says. “They can transmit diseases over great distances and can carry multiple diseases without themselves being sick, and they have very small fangs. You may not even feel the bite or often won’t see a bite wound.”

Because you may not even know you were bitten, it’s imperative that, after any encounter with a bat or any other potentially rabid creature, you immediately go to the ER and get the first of what will likely be a few post-exposure vaccines.

The vaccine is literally the only way to survive if you’ve been infected. There is no “wait and see” window, either.

“Once symptoms manifest, there is no cure for rabies; it has a 100 percent mortality rate and the only way to prevent infection after exposure is through vaccination,” Yuson says.

It’s a scary time, and rabies is a very scary virus, but remember that even with the spike in reported cases of human exposures to rabid or possibly rabid animals, a human dying from rabies is, in the U.S. at least, an incredibly rare thing.

“We average one to six cases of rabies a year in the U.S.,” Rensimer says.

Unfortunately, because of rising temperatures (rabies loves warm weather) and continued encroachment on wildlife habitats by good old mankind (leads to increased exposure risk among humans and pets), rabies doesn’t look to be going anywhere anytime soon.

But thanks to science, there’s no real reason to worry, because if for any reason we do come into contact with a possibly rabid animal, there’s a safe, accessible, and 100 percent effective vaccine available.
